description: Org-level architecture standards: reuse, scope discipline, error handling, data-access boundaries, and API/performance rules that apply to every project installing AI Agile.

standards.title: Reuse before writing new code
standards.description: Before implementing new logic, search the codebase for existing functions, classes, or modules that already solve the same problem or a close approximation of it. Extend existing code rather than duplicating it.
standards.rationale: Duplicate logic diverges over time, creates inconsistent behaviour, and multiplies the maintenance surface. The codebase already contains tested, deployed solutions — use them.
acceptance_criteria: No function or method in the diff duplicates logic that is already present in another module at the time of writing.
If an existing utility solves 80%+ of the need, the diff extends or calls that utility rather than reimplementing the behaviour from scratch.
Any deliberate duplication includes an inline comment explaining why the existing implementation could not be reused.
anti_patterns: Copying a block from one module and pasting it with minor edits into another.
Reimplementing a sort, filter, or transformation already present in a sibling module.
Creating a new helper that is functionally equivalent to an existing one with a different name.

standards.title: Abstract only at two concrete call sites
standards.description: Do not create helpers, base classes, mixins, decorators, or utility modules unless they have at least two distinct, concrete call sites in the codebase at the time of writing. Three similar lines of code are not sufficient justification for a new abstraction.
standards.rationale: Premature abstractions introduce indirection that obscures intent, makes code harder to read, and must be maintained even when requirements change. A duplication that is removed too early often results in an abstraction that fits neither call site well.
acceptance_criteria: Every new function, class, or module introduced in the diff has at least two concrete, distinct call sites visible in the repo at the time the PR is written.
New base classes and mixins have at least two concrete subclasses in the diff or the existing codebase.
New decorator or wrapper functions are applied to at least two target functions in the diff or existing codebase.
anti_patterns: A helper function called only once.
A base class with exactly one subclass.
A utility module with a single export used by a single caller.
Extracting a two-line block into a named function 'for readability' when the block is only used once.

standards.title: No speculative generality
standards.description: Do not add parameters, configuration options, plugin hooks, strategy objects, or extension points for anticipated future requirements that have no current specification in the product docs or active issues. Solve the problem as stated, not a generalised version of it.
standards.rationale: Speculative features are never free — they add complexity, surface area for bugs, and cognitive load for future readers, even if they are never actually used. YAGNI (You Aren't Gonna Need It) applies to every layer of the stack.
acceptance_criteria: Every parameter, config key, and extension point introduced in the diff is exercised by at least one real call site in the same diff or existing codebase.
Optional parameters whose only caller always passes the default value are removed or never introduced.
No code path exists in the diff that is not reachable from any call site present at the time of writing.
Abstract base classes, interfaces, and protocols are only introduced when multiple concrete implementations exist or are required by the current issue's acceptance criteria.
anti_patterns: Adding a `strategy=` or `backend=` parameter with only one value ever passed.
A plugin registry or hook system with zero registered plugins in the diff.
A config flag that is always `True` or always `False` at every call site.
An abstract method defined 'for future subclasses' with no current implementation.

standards.title: Implementations scope to stated acceptance criteria
standards.description: Every line of new behaviour in a diff must be traceable to an acceptance criterion in the approved PRD, an existing standard in this file, or an approved ADR. Behaviour that is not required by any of these sources must not be introduced.
standards.rationale: Out-of-scope additions bypass product approval gates, make PRs harder to review, and risk introducing untested behaviour into production. Scope creep in code is the dual of scope creep in planning.
acceptance_criteria: For each new behaviour visible in the diff, the coder can cite the PRD acceptance criterion, STD ID, or ADR ID that requires it.
No new user-visible behaviour (API surface, config keys, labels, log output) exists in the diff without a corresponding PRD acceptance criterion.
New constants, flags, and configuration fields introduced for a current feature are marked clearly as belonging to that feature, not designed as general infrastructure.
anti_patterns: Adding concurrency controls when the issue only asks for retry logic.
Introducing a metrics endpoint when the issue asks for a config change.
Adding a CLI flag 'while we're here' that is not in the PRD.

standards.title: Keep functions and modules focused
standards.description: Functions should do one thing. Modules should own one concern. When a function grows beyond approximately 40 lines or handles more than one distinct responsibility, split it. When a module imports from more than two unrelated domains, consider splitting it.
standards.rationale: Small, focused units are easier to test, easier to reuse, and easier to reason about. Long functions with multiple responsibilities are the primary source of hidden coupling.
acceptance_criteria: No new function in the diff exceeds 50 lines (excluding docstring and blank lines) unless the lines are a single flat sequence with no branching — e.g. a long match/switch statement.
Functions introduced in the diff have a single clearly-stated purpose that can be described in one sentence without using 'and'.
No module introduced in the diff imports from more than three unrelated domains at the same abstraction level.
anti_patterns: A function named `process_and_validate_and_save()`.
A 200-line function containing distinct phases separated by blank lines and comments.
A module that is both a data model and a network client.

standards.title: Fix now, not later — no deferred small defects
standards.description: If a defect, inconsistency, dead code path, stale comment, incorrect type annotation, or other small correctness issue is visible while working on a diff, fix it in the same PR rather than deferring it. Do not introduce or perpetuate TODO/FIXME markers for issues that can be resolved immediately.
standards.rationale: Small deferred items compound. A codebase full of acknowledged-but-unresolved defects degrades reviewer confidence, slows onboarding, and creates a ratchet where each PR adds more debt than it removes. The cheapest time to fix a defect is when you are already reading the affected code.
acceptance_criteria: No TODO or FIXME comment is introduced in the diff unless it references an open issue number (e.g. '# TODO(#123)') and the linked issue is created before the PR is merged.
Existing TODO/FIXME comments in files touched by the diff are either resolved inline or converted to tracked issues — they are not left as-is.
Dead code (unreachable branches, unused imports, unused variables) visible in files touched by the diff is removed rather than left in place.
Stale inline comments that describe behaviour that no longer exists are removed or corrected.
Type annotations that are visibly wrong or missing on functions touched by the diff are corrected.
A fix is only deferred when the coder documents in the PR description exactly why it cannot be resolved in this PR and links a follow-up issue.
anti_patterns: Adding '# TODO: clean this up later' without an issue number.
Leaving an unreachable `else` branch in a function you are modifying.
Removing a feature but leaving its import and dead helper function.
Correcting a bug in one call site but leaving identical buggy code in the sibling call site in the same file.
Commenting out code instead of deleting it.
Leaving a `pass` or `raise NotImplementedError` in a method that is called in the current execution path.

standards.title: Do not open issues for work that can be done in the current PR
standards.description: Agents must not file new GitHub issues as a substitute for doing work that is within their current scope. If a defect, missing test, incomplete implementation, or related improvement is small enough to be resolved inside the current PR, resolve it there. Creating a new issue is only justified when the work requires a separate product decision, a different owner, a human gate, or a scope that is genuinely outside the current issue's acceptance criteria.
standards.rationale: Issue creation is not free. Every new issue added to the backlog consumes triage time, clutters the pipeline, and is statistically unlikely to be resolved — most small 'follow-up' issues are never actioned. Agents that defer solvable work into new issues are shifting cost onto humans and future pipeline runs.
acceptance_criteria: No new GitHub issue is created by an agent for a defect or gap that is visible in the current diff and resolvable within the current issue's acceptance criteria.
No new GitHub issue is created for work that would be completed in fewer than 30 lines of code and has no dependency on a human gate or external decision.
When an agent creates a new issue, the PR description explains specifically why the work cannot be done inline and what external dependency or decision blocks it.
Agents do not split a single coherent feature into multiple issues to reduce the scope of their current run.
anti_patterns: Opening a 'follow-up' issue for a missing test when the test could be written in the current PR.
Creating an issue titled 'Clean up X' for code touched in the current diff.
Filing an issue for a one-line bug fix found while implementing the current feature.
Splitting 'implement feature' and 'document feature' into separate issues when documentation is an acceptance criterion of the feature.
Creating a placeholder issue with no acceptance criteria as a way to acknowledge tech debt without fixing it.

standards.title: Derive data structure from a single nominated authoritative source
standards.description: Field definitions, column names, data types, and labels are derived at runtime or build time from a single authoritative source of truth, never hardcoded in code that must then be kept in sync with it. Each project nominates that source -- the database schema, a configuration or schema file, or an equivalent registry -- in a project ADR at project start, and all schema-dependent code derives from it.
standards.rationale: Hardcoded field and type definitions silently diverge from the real source and break schema-driven behaviour; a single nominated source keeps generated UI, validation, and serialisation consistent.
acceptance_criteria: Schema-derived code in the diff reads field, type, and label definitions from the project's nominated authoritative source, not hardcoded literals.
No competing hardcoded copy of the schema is introduced alongside the nominated source.
anti_patterns: Hardcoding a field list, column names, or type mappings in a component or module instead of deriving them from the nominated authoritative source.
standards.source: Generalised to org from a project-migrated standard

standards.title: Satisfy a declared return/interface contract completely on every path
standards.description: When a function or handler declares a return or interface contract, every return path -- including error and early-return paths -- produces the complete required shape, never a partial or bare value.
standards.rationale: Consumers rely on the full contract; a return path that produces a partial shape yields a silently-incomplete result downstream.
acceptance_criteria: Every return path of a function/handler with a declared contract in the diff produces the complete required shape (all required fields set).
Error and early-return paths satisfy the same contract (e.g. a well-formed failure object), not a bare, undefined, or partial value.
anti_patterns: Returning a partial object from one branch of a function whose declared contract requires the full shape.
standards.source: Generalised to org from a project-migrated standard

standards.title: Fail closed on errors
standards.description: On an error -- a failed query, a failed external call, or any operation that did not succeed -- fail closed: surface or throw the error. Do not silently swallow it and return a degraded, partial, or success-shaped result as if it succeeded.
standards.rationale: Silently swallowing an error produces a degraded result that looks valid downstream, hiding integrity and availability failures.
acceptance_criteria: Every fallible operation in the diff checks its error/result and stops or throws on failure rather than continuing.
No catch block in the diff swallows an error and returns a success-shaped or default value without re-raising or recording the failure.
A degraded result is emitted only where an explicit, documented fallback is required by the issue.
anti_patterns: Discarding an error return or exception and returning an empty or default value as though the operation succeeded.
standards.source: Generalised to org from a project-migrated standard

standards.title: Verify framework APIs and conventions against existing usage before relying on them
standards.description: Before using a framework or library API, parameter, or convention that is not already established in the codebase, confirm it against the framework's types or an existing usage rather than assuming it must work a certain way. If there is no precedent and no type to back it, verify before shipping.
standards.rationale: Assuming an API or convention exists in a particular form, without checking, ships runtime-breaking code that type-checking and review miss.
acceptance_criteria: A framework API, parameter, or convention used in the diff that has no precedent in the codebase is confirmed against the framework's types or an existing usage.
The diff does not rely on a framework value or parameter inferred from first principles with no precedent or type to back it.
anti_patterns: Calling a library API with an assumed signature or option that is not backed by its types or any existing usage in the codebase.
standards.source: Generalised to org from a project-migrated standard

standards.title: Access data through a middleware or API layer, never directly from the client
standards.description: Client and front-end code must never connect to the database or data store directly. All data access goes through a middleware or API layer that centralises entitlements and authorization, security controls (validation, sanitisation, audit), and performance capabilities (caching, query shaping, limits). The specific middleware or API-layer design is specified in a project ADR early in the project, and all data access routes through it.
standards.rationale: A single data-access layer keeps authorization, validation, auditing, and performance controls uniform; direct client-to-database access bypasses them and couples clients to storage structure.
acceptance_criteria: Client/front-end code in the diff accesses data only through the project's nominated middleware/API layer, never a direct database connection or raw query.
New data-access paths route through the layer so entitlements, validation, and auditing are applied uniformly.
anti_patterns: Client code issuing a raw database query or opening a direct database connection, bypassing the API/middleware layer.
standards.source: Generalised to org from a project-migrated standard

standards.title: Change state through a dedicated validated transition, not a generic update
standards.description: Lifecycle and status fields change only through a dedicated, validated state-transition path -- never an ad-hoc field update -- so transitions are checked against the allowed set, fire their side-effects, and are audited distinctly.
standards.rationale: Mutating state via a generic update bypasses transition validation, side-effects, and the distinct audit trail, and allows invalid states.
acceptance_criteria: Lifecycle/status fields in the diff change through a dedicated, validated transition path, not a generic update payload.
An invalid or unlisted transition is rejected, not written.
anti_patterns: Setting a status or lifecycle field with a generic update call instead of an explicit, validated transition.
standards.source: Generalised to org from a project-migrated standard

standards.title: Use a consistent API response envelope
standards.description: API responses use a single, documented envelope with uniform shapes: success responses share a consistent structure and error responses a consistent error structure. Endpoints do not invent ad-hoc, per-endpoint response shapes.
standards.rationale: A uniform envelope lets every consumer parse responses the same way; ad-hoc shapes break clients and leak internal structure.
acceptance_criteria: Responses in the diff use the project's standard success and error envelope, not a bespoke per-endpoint shape.
Error responses use the consistent error structure rather than an ad-hoc shape.
anti_patterns: Returning a bespoke JSON shape from one endpoint that differs from the project's standard success/error envelope.
standards.source: Generalised to org from a project-migrated standard

standards.title: Never expose raw internal database identifiers; expose stable external IDs
standards.description: Raw database primary and foreign keys are never exposed through any external channel -- web UI, API responses, exports, logs, or tool input/output. Expose a stable external identifier instead. The external-identifier scheme is a project decision.
standards.rationale: Raw internal keys leak storage structure and are unstable across environments; a stable external identifier decouples consumers from the database and avoids enumerable-ID exposure.
acceptance_criteria: No diff surfaces a raw primary or foreign key through any channel -- UI, API response, export, log, or tool I/O.
Identifier values crossing an external boundary in the diff use the project's stable external-identifier scheme.
anti_patterns: Returning a raw numeric or UUID primary key in an API response, URL, export, or log line.
standards.source: Generalised to org from a project-migrated standard

standards.title: Do not use deprecated language or DSL constructs; use the current supported form
standards.description: Code and DSL/expression authoring use the current, supported syntax and APIs -- not deprecated ones that emit warnings or are scheduled for removal.
standards.rationale: Deprecated constructs warn now and break later; using the current supported form keeps code forward-compatible.
acceptance_criteria: The diff does not introduce a deprecated language, DSL, or API construct where a current supported form exists.
Deprecated constructs in code or expressions touched by the diff are migrated to the current form.
anti_patterns: Using a deprecated API or language/DSL construct when a current supported form exists.
standards.source: Generalised to org from a project-migrated standard

standards.title: Avoid N+1 queries and unbounded reads; respect platform query limits
standards.description: Avoid N+1 query patterns -- bulk-fetch related data by deduplicating IDs into a single query rather than one query per record -- and bound large reads with pagination, respecting the data platform's row limits.
standards.rationale: Per-record fetches produce N+1 query storms, and a silent default row cap truncates large reads.
acceptance_criteria: Related-data fetches in the diff collect and deduplicate IDs and issue a single bulk query, not one per record.
Reads against potentially-large tables use pagination rather than relying on the platform's default row cap.
No diff issues a query inside a per-record loop where a single bulk query would suffice.
anti_patterns: Issuing one query per record in a loop instead of a single bulk query; reading an unbounded result set without pagination.
standards.source: Generalised to org from a project-migrated standard

standards.title: Do not use `as any`/non-null assertions to silence the type system at the data boundary
standards.description: Type assertions that defeat the compiler -- `as any`, double casts, and non-null assertions -- must not be used to force values across a data boundary. Where a value's runtime shape differs from its static type, validate or convert it explicitly rather than asserting.
standards.rationale: Assertions that defeat the compiler hide real shape mismatches at data boundaries; correcting the type or validating the value surfaces them.
acceptance_criteria: No diff introduces `as any` or a double cast to push a value across a data boundary.
No diff adds a non-null assertion to suppress a nullability or shape error instead of handling it.
Where a declared type mismatches the runtime shape, the diff fixes the type or parses/validates the value rather than casting.
anti_patterns: Using `as any` or a non-null assertion to force a value across the data boundary instead of validating it.
standards.source: Generalised to org from a project-migrated standard
